title: Best Proofreaders and Editors (2026): How to Hire One
description: How to hire a proofreader or editor: which level of editing you need, what to send, what drives the price and the red flags to avoid.
intro: A proofreader catches errors; an editor improves how the writing reads. Many disappointing orders come from buying the wrong level: a quick proofread for text that needed real editing, or heavy editing that changed a voice the writer wanted to keep. This guide explains the levels and how to order the right one.

faq.q: What is the difference between proofreading and editing?
faq.a: Proofreading fixes spelling, grammar, punctuation and typos in finished text. Copy editing also improves clarity, consistency and word choice. Developmental or structural editing looks at the content and organization as a whole. Each level takes more time and costs more.

faq.q: Will I see what was changed?
faq.a: Ask for tracked changes in Word or suggestions in Google Docs. You can then accept or reject each change and learn from the edits.
Tell the editor which one, or which style guide you follow. Spelling, punctuation and some words differ, and mixing them looks careless.
Some do as an extra, but it is not part of normal proofreading. If accuracy matters, ask for fact-checking specifically or check facts yourself.
Ask before sending. For unpublished books, business documents or academic work, check how the editor stores files and whether they use AI tools on your text.
